posts.title: Publish a brand kit (before someone scrapes your favicon)
posts.summary: What belongs on a public brand kit / media kit page, how to SEO it, and examples from Wikimedia, Mozilla, GitHub — plus our own kit at /brand.
posts.html:
If a journalist, partner, or sibling OSS org needs your logo at 11pm, they will take whatever loads first: a 16×16 favicon, a Facebook avatar, or an Incapsula HTML error saved as .png. That is not a brand strategy. It is what happens when you teach “make a brand kit” and never publish one.

This guide is the operator checklist. Use it to ship a brand kit, media kit, or press kit page — logos, colors, type, usage — on your domain. Then point every “for press / partners” ask at that URL.

Start here: our kit

Nonprofit Resources brand kit (/brand) is the working example for this site:

  • Logo SVG/PNG downloads (tiled mark and mark-only)

  • Color palette with copyable hex

  • Typography (Plus Jakarta Sans)

  • Name, voice, and usage rules

  • SEO aliases for media kit, press kit, brand guidelines, style guide, and logo

Canonical URL: https://nonprofit-resources.org/brand.

What to put on the page

Keep one job per section. Visitors should leave with files and rules, not a slide deck about “our journey.”

  • Logos — SVG first, PNG fallbacks at useful sizes (256 for avatars). Light and dark grounds if the mark inverts.

  • Colors — named roles (primary, accent, ground) with hex. Optional CSS variable names if you ship a product UI.

  • Typography — family, stack, and a link to the licensed source (Google Fonts, Adobe, or your webfont zip).

  • Name & voice — full legal/product name, short form, domain, one paragraph on tone.

  • Usage — clear space, no stretch, no fake endorsement, contact for exceptions.

  • Downloads — real <a download> links, not a “email us for assets” form.

That package is the media kit. Press kit and brand guidelines are the same page with better headings — do not invent three empty microsites.

SEO the boring words on purpose

People search the synonyms, not your internal folder name. Put them in the title, lead, and meta description:

  • brand kit · media kit · press kit

  • brand guidelines · style guide · branding

  • logo download · SVG · PNG · favicon

  • color palette · typography

Use one canonical URL (we use /brand) and optional aliases that share the page. Do not thin-out five duplicate articles.

Examples worth copying

These orgs publish assets instead of hoping the favicon CDN is kind:

  • Wikimedia Brand — portal for logo, type, color, templates, and trademark pointers. Movement-scale, still a single front door.

  • Mozilla Trademark Guidelines — rules first; pair with public Protocol assets when you need files. Trademarks and downloads are not the same document, but both exist.

  • GitHub Logos and Usage — permitted marks, do/don’t, and downloads for integrations.

  • U.S. Web Design System (USWDS) — government design system with tokens and components; useful when your “brand” is also a product UI.

  • Nonprofit Resources brand kit — small-org version of the same idea: one page, downloads, no bot wall.

Steal the shape, not the lockup. Your mark stays yours.

The TechSoup footnote

TechSoup’s own brand-management guide tells nonprofits to create style guides and shared asset libraries. As of this writing they still have no public branding page or media kit — and techsoup.org/favicon.ico answers with a bot challenge instead of an icon. We note that on their catalog entries (Product Donations, Software Directory) and keep our assets on /brand so partners are not hunting social avatars.

Irony is not the product. The product is a URL that returns SVG.

Ship checklist

  • ❏ Page live on your primary domain (not only Google Drive)

  • ❏ SVG + PNG for the primary mark; favicon matches the mark

  • ❏ Hex list copyable; typeface licensed and linked

  • ❏ Usage paragraph that forbids implied endorsement

  • ❏ Title and description include brand kit / media kit / logo language

  • ❏ Footer or About links to the kit in one click

  • ❏ Someone outside your team can download a logo without asking Slack

When that list is green, the next partner who needs your logo at midnight will thank you — and your catalog neighbors will too.

posts.title: Keep the catalog in sync
posts.summary: Pull our JSON catalog, or register a webhook, when sibling directories such as OSS.Fund change.
posts.html:
Open-source projects are a subset of the orgs this catalog serves. OSS.Fund is the sibling directory for OSS funding platforms (Open Collective, GitHub Sponsors, Liberapay, and the rest). They do not offer an HTTP API or webhooks. Their public source is Markdown on GitHub (CC BY 4.0): oss-fund/directory.

This site therefore:

  1. Lists OSS.Fund itself as a meta-directory.

  2. Imports live OSS-friendly / nonprofit-tagged platforms into the Open source category (pnpm catalog:sync-oss-fund).

  3. Publishes a pull API so they — or anyone — can consume our catalog.

  4. Offers outbound catalog.updated webhooks, plus an inbound GitHub receiver if OSS.Fund (or we) attach a repo webhook later.

Pull the catalog

JSON feed (CORS enabled, 5-minute cache):

GET https://nonprofit-resources.org/api/catalog

Each item includes id, slug, name, href, category, tags, portalUrl, openSource, and verification flags. Filter items where openSource is true for the OSS subset.

Attribution

Imported OSS.Fund rows stay attributed in each listing and on /attributions. If you republish those rows, keep the CC BY 4.0 credit to OSS.Fund.

Outbound webhooks

Staff (signed-in admin email or CATALOG_WEBHOOK_ADMIN_TOKEN) can register a destination:

curl -X POST https://nonprofit-resources.org/api/webhooks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CATALOG_WEBHOOK_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"url":"https://example.org/hooks/nr","note":"oss.fund mirror"}'

The response includes a secret once. Every later POST is HMAC-SHA256:

  • Header X-Nonprofit-Resources-Event: catalog.updated

  • Header X-Nonprofit-Resources-Signature: sha256=<hex>

  • JSON body with catalog (URL of /api/catalog) and occurredAt

Production deploys call /api/webhooks/dispatch with CATALOG_WEBHOOK_DISPATCH_SECRET. Polling /api/catalog is enough if you do not want a push.

Private/loopback URLs are rejected.

Inbound GitHub webhook (OSS.Fund)

If the maintainers of oss-fund/directory add a webhook:

  • Payload URL: https://nonprofit-resources.org/api/webhooks/github

  • Content type: application/json

  • Secret: the same value as OSS_FUND_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET

  • Events: Pushes

That ping starts GitHub Actions (repository_dispatch: oss-fund-sync), which regenerates src/lib/oss-fund-seed.generated.ts and opens a PR. A daily cron does the same when no webhook is attached.

Until they add that hook, we stay in sync by cloning their repo on a schedule.

Sending listings the other way

OSS.Fund accepts new platforms as a pull request against posts/ in oss-fund/directory. A listing for Nonprofit Resources belongs there as a directory, not a funding platform, and should wait on their editorial review. Prefer that they poll /api/catalog if they want the full feed.

Related

  • Browse locally: /services?oss=1

  • Script: pnpm catalog:sync-oss-fund

  • OSS.Fund about page: oss.fund/about

posts.title: Donate page as a ledger
posts.summary: Show the operating fund, the monthly floor, and the donate button on the same page — instead of a mission sentence and a hop to a third-party form.
posts.html:
Most donation pages hide the books. A visitor sees a mission sentence and a button. They do not see whether last month’s costs are covered, whether the org is sitting on unused cash, or what “enough” even means.

A better ask treats the donate page as a ledger: current balance, the minimum required to keep the service running, an as-of date, and the work that money pays for — then the button.

The pattern (Transparency HOA)

Transparency HOA’s Analyze Queue (a 501(c)(3) founded in 2019) puts the ask on the same page as the work queue.

As captured in 2026, the page states that the Analyze service costs about $6,000 per month, shows an Analysis Fund balance ($7,881 as of 30 April 2026), and keeps Donate Now on that same view. Below the fund, a pending list names the associations waiting for analysis.

Screenshot of the public Analyze Queue page. Used here as a cited example of an on-site fund ask. Source: transparencyhoa.org/analyze-queue.

The numbers will change. The design lesson does not: cost + balance + date + ask + work, on one page, under the org’s own brand.

What to put on the page

  • Floor — the minimum to stay in operation for the period you actually run (monthly burn for a service, quarterly for a slower program). Say what the number includes.

  • Balance or raised — cash on hand for that fund, or amount raised toward a campaign. Label which it is.

  • As-of date — stale totals destroy trust faster than no totals.

  • Ask — donate (or sponsor) in the same view. The payment processor can still be Stripe, Open Collective, or a fiscal host; do not exile the story to a blank third-party form.

  • What the money buys — a queue, a milestone list, a public budget line. Visitors should see work, not only a thermometer.

A goal amount is useful when you are filling a campaign. A floor is more honest when the real question is “can this keep running next month?” You can show both: floor as the line you must not fall under, goal as the next useful surplus.

Why this beats a generic donate button

  • Trust — published numbers beat “please support our mission.”

  • Urgency without theater — a balance near the floor is a reason to give; a surplus is also honest (the example above was above one month of burn).

  • Ownership — the ask stays on your site. Hosted fundraisers are fine as the checkout rail, not as the only page a donor ever sees.

This works for 501(c) organizations and for donation-supported products or OSS projects. The legal wrapper changes the tax receipt; it does not change the UX.

What not to fake

  • Do not invent a burn rate. If you do not know monthly cost, publish a smaller true number (hosting only) rather than a rounded “we need $X.”

  • Do not hide a large reserve behind a crisis headline.

  • Do not copy another org’s dollar figures into your own page.

  • Tax deductibility, fiscal-host fees, and charitable status are jurisdiction-specific. This guide is a page pattern, not legal or accounting advice.

Related
